notes.front: What is constructive receipt of income?
notes.back: For a cash-method taxpayer, income is generally taxed when it is available to you, even if you have not taken possession of it.
notes.explanation: Publication 525 says a cash-method taxpayer is generally taxed on income that is available, regardless of whether it is actually in hand.
notes.example: Like a pay cheque that is waiting for you at the office on 31 December: you could have collected it, so it counts that year even if you pick it up in January.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Constructively received income”, p. 2
notes.evidence: If you're a cash-method taxpayer, you're generally taxed on income that is available to you, regardless of whether it is actually in your possession.

notes.front: What is a qualified dividend?
notes.back: An ordinary dividend taxed at the same 0%, 15% or 20% maximum rates that apply to net capital gain.
notes.explanation: The qualified part of your ordinary dividends gets the lower capital gain rates instead of ordinary income tax rates.
notes.example: Like an ordinary dividend from a company share, but the part the payer marks as qualified is taxed at the capital gain rates.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Qualified Dividends”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Qualified dividends are the ordinary dividends that are subject to the same 0%, 15%, or 20% maximum tax rate that applies to net capital gain.

notes.front: What is a capital gain distribution?
notes.back: A distribution (capital gain dividend) paid by a mutual fund or real estate investment trust out of its capital gains.
notes.explanation: Mutual funds (and other regulated investment companies) and real estate investment trusts pay them, and they are shown on the payer's dividend statement.
notes.example: Like the year-end payout a stock fund makes after selling shares at a profit inside the fund.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Gain Distributions”, p. 30
notes.evidence: Capital gain distributions (capital gain dividends) are paid to you or credited to your account by mutual funds (or other regulated investment companies) and real estate investment trusts (REITs).

notes.front: What does Form 1099-DIV report?
notes.back: Dividends paid to you: ordinary dividends in box 1a, capital gain distributions in box 2a, nondividend distributions in box 3.
notes.explanation: The payer (a corporation or fund) sends it; box numbers tell you which kind of distribution each amount is.
notes.example: Like a year-end summary from your brokerage for a fund you hold, split into boxes by type of payout.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Ordinary Dividends”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Ordinary dividends will be shown on Form 1099-DIV, box 1a.

notes.front: What is cancellation of debt (COD) income?
notes.back: Income you are generally treated as having when a lender cancels or forgives a debt for less than its full amount.
notes.explanation: Publication 4681 calls debt canceled, forgiven or discharged for less than the full amount "canceled debt", and it may be taxable.
notes.example: Like a credit card company accepting a smaller lump sum to close your account: the part it writes off is canceled debt.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Generally, if you owe a debt to someone else and they cancel or forgive that debt for less than its full amount, you are treated for income tax purposes as having income and may have to pay tax on this income.

notes.front: What is qualified principal residence indebtedness?
notes.back: A mortgage you took out to buy, build or substantially improve your main home, secured by that home.
notes.explanation: It also covers debt secured by the main home used to refinance such a mortgage, but only up to the old mortgage principal.
notes.example: Like the loan you took to buy the house you live in, but not a loan secured by a holiday home.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Qualified Principal Residence Indebtedness”, p. 9
notes.evidence: Qualified principal residence indebtedness is any mortgage you took out to buy, build, or substantially improve your main home. It must also be secured by your main home.

notes.front: When are you insolvent, for the canceled-debt rules?
notes.back: When your total liabilities are more than the fair market value of all your assets, immediately before the cancellation.
notes.explanation: Insolvency is measured at one moment, immediately before the debt is canceled, and only to the extent liabilities exceed assets.
notes.example: Like owing $80,000 in total when everything you own would sell for $60,000: you are insolvent by $20,000.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Insolvency”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You were insolvent immediately before the cancellation to the extent that the total of all of your liabilities was more than the FMV of all of your assets immediately before the cancellation.

notes.front: What is the tax benefit rule?
notes.back: A recovery is income in the year received, up to the amount by which the earlier deduction or credit reduced your tax.
notes.explanation: A recovery is the return of an amount you deducted or took a credit for earlier; the rule taxes it only as far as the earlier deduction actually helped.
notes.example: Like getting back part of a medical bill you deducted last year: you count it only to the extent last year's deduction lowered your tax.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Recoveries”, p. 24
notes.evidence: You must include a recovery in your income in the year you receive it up to the amount by which the deduction or credit you took for the recovered amount reduced your tax in the earlier year.

notes.front: Where does a net operating loss (NOL) from an earlier year show up on a 2025 return?
notes.back: As an NOL deduction on Schedule 1, line 8a, entered as a negative number.
notes.explanation: The deduction is subtracted from the other income amounts on lines 8b through 8z; Form 172 and its instructions give the details.
notes.example: Like a business owner whose big loss in an earlier year was more than that year's income, carrying the unused loss forward to reduce this year's income.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Schedule 1, line 8a: Net operating loss (NOL) deduction”, p. 91
notes.evidence: Net operating loss (NOL) deduction. Enter any deduction for an NOL from an earlier year. Enter the amount in the preprinted parentheses (as a negative number).

notes.front: What is a constructive dividend (what Publication 550 calls a constructive distribution)?
notes.back: A transaction that increases your proportionate interest in a corporation and is treated as if it were a distribution to you.
notes.explanation: Publication 550 says these constructive distributions are taxable when they have the same result as the taxable stock distributions it lists.
notes.example: Like a change in your preferred stock's conversion ratio that gives you a bigger share of the company without any payment changing hands.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Distributions of Stock and Stock Rights: Constructive distributions”, p. 31
notes.evidence: You must treat certain transactions that increase your proportionate interest in the earnings and profits or assets of a corporation as if they were distributions of stock or stock rights.

notes.front: What are the two kinds of passive activity?
notes.back: Trade or business activities you don't materially participate in; and rental activities, even with material participation, unless you're a real estate professional.
notes.explanation: Publication 925 defines passive activities as exactly these two kinds.
notes.example: Like owning a share of a restaurant you never work in, or renting out a flat you own.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Passive Activities”, p. 4
notes.evidence: There are two kinds of passive activities. • Trade or business activities in which you don't materially participate during the year. • Rental activities, even if you do materially participate in them, unless you're a real estate professional.

notes.front: What is material participation in a trade or business activity?
notes.back: Meeting any one of the tests in Publication 925, such as working in the activity for more than 500 hours in the year.
notes.explanation: Satisfying any single test is enough, and a business you materially participate in is not a passive activity.
notes.example: Like a part-owner of a bakery who works there most weekdays all year, well over 500 hours.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Material participation tests”, p. 7
notes.evidence: You materially participated in a trade or business activity for a tax year if you satisfy any of the following tests. 1. You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours.

notes.front: What does a partner get on Schedule K-1 (Form 1065)?
notes.back: Their share of the partnership's income, deductions, credits and tax preference items for the year.
notes.explanation: Each partnership sends one to each partner; the partner keeps it and reports the items on their own return.
notes.example: Like a statement from a two-person consulting partnership telling each partner their half of the year's profit.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Partnership Income: Schedule K-1 (Form 1065)”, p. 17
notes.evidence: You should receive from each partnership in which you're a member a copy of Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) showing your share of income, deductions, credits, and tax preference items of the partnership for the tax year.

notes.front: What is an individual retirement arrangement (IRA)?
notes.back: A personal savings plan that gives you tax advantages for setting aside money for retirement.
notes.explanation: Its two main advantages are that contributions may be deductible and that earnings are generally not taxed until distributed.
notes.example: Like a savings account you open at a bank or broker, but with tax rules that reward leaving the money there until retirement.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Introduction”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An IRA is a personal savings plan that gives you tax advantages for setting aside money for retirement.

notes.front: What is a Roth IRA?
notes.back: An IRA to which contributions are not deductible, but whose qualified distributions are tax free.
notes.explanation: Publication 590-A says it is subject to the traditional IRA rules except where its own chapter says otherwise.
notes.example: Like a traditional IRA turned around: you pay tax on the money going in, and qualified withdrawals come out tax free.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What Is a Roth IRA?”, p. 39
notes.evidence: Unlike a traditional IRA, you can't deduct contributions to a Roth IRA. But, if you satisfy the requirements, qualified distributions (discussed in chapter 2 of Pub. 590-B) are tax free

notes.front: What is a rollover?
notes.back: A tax-free distribution of cash or assets from one retirement plan that you contribute to another retirement plan within 60 days.
notes.explanation: The contribution to the second plan is called a rollover contribution; the money is generally taxed later when it comes out of the second plan.
notes.example: Like cashing out your old employer's plan and depositing the full amount in an IRA five weeks later.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Rollovers”, p. 22
notes.evidence: Generally, a rollover is a tax-free distribution to you of cash or other assets from one retirement plan that you contribute to another retirement plan within 60 days you received the payment or distribution.

notes.front: What is a qualified charitable distribution (QCD)?
notes.back: A generally nontaxable distribution paid directly by your IRA trustee to a charity eligible for deductible contributions.
notes.explanation: The trustee pays the charity directly, and you must be at least 70½ when the distribution is made.
notes.example: Like asking your IRA custodian to send a cheque straight to a food bank instead of paying you.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs)”, p. 13
notes.evidence: A QCD is generally a nontaxable distribution made directly by the trustee of your IRA (other than an ongoing SEP or SIMPLE IRA) to an organization eligible to receive tax-deductible contributions.

notes.front: What is an excess contribution to a traditional IRA?
notes.back: The amount contributed for the year above the smaller of the annual limit or your taxable compensation.
notes.explanation: For 2025 the annual limit is $7,000, or $8,000 if you are 50 or older.
notes.example: Like putting $7,000 into your IRA in a year when your only taxable compensation was $5,000 of wages.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Excess Contributions”, p. 35
notes.evidence: Generally, an excess contribution is the amount contributed to your traditional IRAs for the year that is more than the smaller of:

notes.front: What is a prohibited transaction with an IRA?
notes.back: Any improper use of the IRA by you, your beneficiary or any disqualified person.
notes.explanation: Disqualified persons include your fiduciary and members of your family: spouse, ancestor, lineal descendant and any spouse of a lineal descendant.
notes.example: Like using money in your IRA to buy a holiday cottage your family stays in.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Prohibited Transactions”, p. 22
notes.evidence: Generally, a prohibited transaction is any improper use of your IRA account or annuity by you, your beneficiary, or any disqualified person.

notes.front: What is a conversion to a Roth IRA?
notes.back: Withdrawing assets from a traditional IRA and reinvesting them in a Roth IRA within 60 days (a conversion contribution).
notes.explanation: Publication 590-A calls the amount withdrawn and timely contributed to the Roth IRA a conversion contribution.
notes.example: Like moving $20,000 of shares from your traditional IRA into your Roth IRA and paying the income tax on the move.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Converting From Any Traditional IRA Into a Roth IRA”, p. 29
notes.evidence: You can withdraw all or part of the assets from a traditional IRA and reinvest them (within 60 days) in a Roth IRA. The amount that you withdraw and timely contribute (convert) to the Roth IRA is called a conversion contribution.

notes.front: What is recharacterization of an IRA contribution?
notes.back: Treating a contribution made to one type of IRA as if it had been made to a different type of IRA.
notes.explanation: It is generally done by a trustee-to-trustee transfer from the first IRA to the second.
notes.example: Like moving this year's Roth IRA contribution to a traditional IRA after learning your income is too high for a Roth.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Recharacterizations”, p. 29
notes.evidence: You may be able to treat a contribution made to one type of IRA as having been made to a different type of IRA. This is called recharacterizing the contribution.

notes.front: What is a required minimum distribution (RMD)?
notes.back: The amount that must be distributed from the IRA each year.
notes.explanation: If you don't take it, you may owe an excise tax on the amount not distributed as required.
notes.example: Like a yearly minimum withdrawal your IRA custodian works out once you reach the starting age.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Required minimum distribution (RMD)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Required minimum distribution (RMD). The amount that must be distributed each year is referred to as the required minimum distribution.

notes.front: What are equivalent tier 1 railroad retirement benefits (RRB)?
notes.back: The part of tier 1 benefits a railroad employee or beneficiary would have received under the social security system.
notes.explanation: Publication 915 treats this part the same as social security benefits; it is commonly called the social security equivalent benefit portion.
notes.example: Like a retired railroad worker's monthly benefit, of which only the social-security-like slice follows these rules.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Equivalent tier 1 railroad retirement benefits are the part of tier 1 benefits that a railroad employee or beneficiary would have been entitled to receive under the social security system.

notes.front: What is an incentive stock option (ISO)?
notes.back: A statutory stock option; you must stay an employee of the grantor, or a related company, from grant until 3 months before exercise.
notes.explanation: For an ISO the period is 1 year before exercise if you are disabled, and the option must be nontransferable except at death.
notes.example: Like a right your employer gives you to buy its shares at today's price for the next ten years, taxed under the special statutory rules.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Statutory Stock Options”, p. 12
notes.evidence: you must be an employee of the company granting the option, or a related company, at all times during the period beginning on the date the option is granted and ending 3 months before the date you exercise the option

notes.front: What is a nonstatutory stock option?
notes.back: An option that isn't statutory; you may have income at grant, depending on whether its fair market value is readily determinable.
notes.explanation: An option you get without meeting the statutory employment rules, or a transferable one, is nonstatutory.
notes.example: Like options a start-up gives an outside consultant: they do not qualify for the statutory rules.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Nonstatutory Stock Options”, p. 11
notes.evidence: If you're granted a nonstatutory stock option, you may have income when you receive the option. The amount of income to include and the time to include it depend on whether the FMV of the option can be readily determined.

notes.front: What is an employee stock purchase plan (ESPP) option?
notes.back: One of the two kinds of statutory stock option, the other being the incentive stock option.
notes.explanation: Both kinds share the same employment and nontransferability requirements.
notes.example: Like a payroll plan that lets staff buy company shares at 90% of market price each quarter.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Statutory Stock Options”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Options granted under employee stock purchase plans.

notes.front: When should a payer send you Form 1099-NEC?
notes.back: When you aren't an employee and its fees to you in the course of its trade or business total $600 or more for the year.
notes.explanation: The fees reported on it may be self-employment income.
notes.example: Like a freelance designer paid $2,000 by a shop for a new logo.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Nonemployee compensation”, p. 77
notes.evidence: If you aren't an employee and the fees for your services from a single payer in the course of the payer's trade or business total $600 or more for the year, the payer should send you a Form 1099-NEC.

notes.front: Must you report wages on Form 1040, line 1a if you never receive a Form W-2?
notes.back: Yes. All pay goes on line 1a even without a Form W-2, or when the Form W-2 leaves some pay out.
notes.explanation: Publication 525 ties the duty to report to the pay itself, not to the form.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Employee Compensation”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Include all your pay on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1a, even if you don't receive Form W-2

notes.front: When are fringe benefits from your employer not included in income?
notes.back: When you pay fair market value for them or the law specifically excludes them.
notes.explanation: Otherwise, fringe benefits received for your services are income as compensation.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Fringe Benefits”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Fringe benefits received in connection with the performance of your services are included in your income as compensation unless you pay FMV for them or they're specifically excluded by law.

notes.front: At year end an employer gives each worker a $50 supermarket gift card. Is it income to the workers?
notes.back: Yes. It is extra wages, whatever the amount.
notes.explanation: A gift certificate or similar item easily exchanged for cash is included as wages regardless of the amount.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Holiday gifts”, p. 5
notes.evidence: if your employer gives you cash, a gift certificate, or a similar item that you can easily exchange for cash, you include the value of that gift as extra salary or wages regardless of the amount involved.

notes.front: Is interest on a state's bond that finances government operations generally taxable?
notes.back: Generally not, if a state, the District of Columbia, a U.S. territory or a political subdivision issued it.
notes.explanation: This is the general tax-exempt interest rule; some state or local bond interest is still taxable.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Tax-Exempt Interest”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Interest on a bond used to finance government operations generally is not taxable if the bond is issued by a state, the District of Columbia, a U.S. territory, or any of their political subdivisions.

notes.front: A credit union's year-end statement calls $120 paid on a member's share account a "dividend". How is it reported?
notes.back: As interest, not as a dividend.
notes.explanation: So-called dividends on deposits or share accounts in credit unions and similar institutions are really interest.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Dividends that are actually interest”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Certain distributions commonly called dividends are actually interest.

notes.front: Out of what are ordinary dividends paid, and how are they taxed?
notes.back: Out of earnings and profits; they are ordinary income, not capital gains.
notes.explanation: Publication 550 calls them the most common type of distribution from a corporation or mutual fund.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Ordinary Dividends”, p. 28
notes.evidence: They are paid out of earnings and profits and are ordinary income to you. This means they are not capital gains.

notes.front: Dana bought mutual fund shares in October 2025. In December the fund paid a capital gain distribution. Is it short-term or long-term gain?
notes.back: Long-term, even though Dana held the shares for about 2 months.
notes.explanation: Capital gain distributions are reported as long-term gains regardless of how long you owned the fund shares.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Gain Distributions”, p. 30
notes.evidence: Report capital gain distributions as long-term capital gains, regardless of how long you owned your shares in the mutual fund or REIT.

notes.front: How are a mutual fund's distributions of net short-term capital gains treated?
notes.back: As ordinary dividends, not capital gains; they are included on Form 1099-DIV as ordinary dividends.
notes.explanation: Only the fund's long-term gains come out as capital gain distributions.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital gain distributions”, p. 34
notes.evidence: the distributions of net realized short-term capital gains are not treated as capital gains. Instead, they are included on Form 1099-DIV as ordinary dividends.

notes.front: How is a nondividend distribution (Form 1099-DIV, box 3) taxed?
notes.back: It reduces your basis in the stock and is not taxed until that basis is fully recovered.
notes.explanation: It is a distribution not paid out of earnings and profits, so it is a return of your investment first.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Nondividend Distributions”, p. 30
notes.evidence: A nondividend distribution reduces the basis of your stock. It is not taxed until your basis in the stock is fully recovered.

notes.front: A Form 1099-DIV shows $400 in box 1a, of which $300 is qualified, and $250 in box 2a. Which amounts get capital gain rates?
notes.back: The $300 of qualified dividends and the $250 capital gain distribution; the other $100 is taxed as ordinary income.
notes.explanation: Qualified dividends share the net capital gain rates; capital gain distributions are long-term gains. $400 − $300 = $100 of ordinary dividends remains at ordinary rates.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Qualified Dividends”, p. 28
notes.evidence: Qualified dividends are the ordinary dividends that are subject to the same 0%, 15%, or 20% maximum tax rate that applies to net capital gain.

notes.front: Where do you report rental income from personal property if you aren't in the business of renting it?
notes.back: On Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8l.
notes.explanation: If you are in that business, income and expenses go on Schedule C instead.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Personal Property Rental”, p. 16
notes.evidence: If you aren't in the business of renting personal property, report your rental income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8l.

notes.front: Where do gambling winnings not from a trade or business go, and are fantasy sports winnings included?
notes.back: Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8b; yes, fantasy sports league winnings are gambling winnings.
notes.explanation: Both are gambling winnings, reported on the same line.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Gambling winnings”, p. 33
notes.evidence: You must include your gambling winnings in your income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8b. Winnings from fantasy sports leagues are gambling winnings.

notes.front: Sam wins a car worth $32,000 in a charity raffle. What must Sam include in income?
notes.back: The car's fair market value, $32,000, as gambling winnings.
notes.explanation: Raffle winnings are gambling winnings, and noncash prizes are included at fair market value.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Lotteries and raffles”, p. 33
notes.evidence: Winnings from lotteries and raffles are gambling winnings. In addition to cash winnings, you must include in your income the FMV of bonds, cars, houses, and other noncash prizes.

notes.front: How may a casual gambler deduct gambling losses?
notes.back: Only by itemizing on Schedule A, and only up to the amount of gambling winnings.
notes.explanation: The losses are an itemized deduction capped at the year's winnings.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Gambling winnings”, p. 33
notes.evidence: If you itemize your deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040), you can deduct gambling losses you had during the year, but only up to the amount of your winnings.

notes.front: Lee, who itemizes, won $3,000 and lost $5,000 gambling in 2025. What goes in income, and what loss is deductible?
notes.back: $3,000 of winnings in income; $3,000 of losses deductible on Schedule A.
notes.explanation: Losses are deductible only up to winnings: the smaller of $5,000 losses and $3,000 winnings is $3,000. The other $2,000 of loss is not deductible.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Gambling winnings”, p. 33
notes.evidence: If you itemize your deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040), you can deduct gambling losses you had during the year, but only up to the amount of your winnings.

notes.front: For 2018 through 2025, what limit applies to a professional gambler's losses and expenses?
notes.back: They are limited to the amount of gambling winnings; the business is reported on Schedule C.
notes.explanation: A trade or business of gambling uses Schedule C, but the same winnings cap applies to losses and expenses.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Gambling winnings”, p. 33
notes.evidence: If you're in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040). For tax years 2018 through 2025, professional gambling losses and expenses are limited to the amount of your winnings.

notes.front: A card issuer accepts $4,000 to settle Pat's $10,000 balance in 2025. Pat was solvent and not in bankruptcy. How much is canceled debt income?
notes.explanation: $10,000 owed − $4,000 paid = $6,000 forgiven. A debt canceled for less than its full amount is generally income, and no exclusion applies here.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Generally, if you owe a debt to someone else and they cancel or forgive that debt for less than its full amount, you are treated for income tax purposes as having income

notes.front: How do you report a debt canceled in a title 11 bankruptcy case?
notes.back: Attach Form 982, check line 1a, and enter the total debt canceled in the case on line 2.
notes.explanation: You must also reduce your tax attributes in Part II of Form 982.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Bankruptcy”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Enter the total amount of debt canceled in your title 11 bankruptcy case on line 2. You must also reduce your tax attributes in Part II of Form 982

notes.front: A farmer's qualified farm debt is canceled in a title 11 bankruptcy case. Which exclusion applies?
notes.back: The bankruptcy exclusion, not the qualified farm debt exclusion.
notes.explanation: Publication 4681 says a title 11 cancellation of qualified farm debt must use the bankruptcy exclusion.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Qualified Farm Indebtedness”, p. 8
notes.evidence: If qualified farm debt is canceled in a title 11 case, you must apply the bankruptcy exclusion rather than the exclusion for canceled qualified farm debt.

notes.front: On Form 982, what do you enter on line 2 for the insolvency exclusion?
notes.back: The smaller of the debt canceled or the amount by which you were insolvent; you also check line 1b.
notes.explanation: The Insolvency Worksheet in Publication 4681 helps you work out the amount of insolvency.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “How to report the insolvency exclusion”, p. 6
notes.evidence: On line 2, include the smaller of the amount of the debt canceled or the amount by which you were insolvent immediately before the cancellation.

notes.front: Just before a $15,000 debt was canceled, Chris had liabilities of $50,000 and assets worth $38,000. How much of the $15,000 is excluded?
notes.back: $12,000 is excluded; $3,000 is income.
notes.explanation: $50,000 − $38,000 = $12,000 of insolvency. The exclusion is the smaller of $15,000 and $12,000, so $15,000 − $12,000 = $3,000 stays in income.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “How to report the insolvency exclusion”, p. 6
notes.evidence: On line 2, include the smaller of the amount of the debt canceled or the amount by which you were insolvent immediately before the cancellation.

notes.front: Qualified principal residence indebtedness can be excluded from income for discharges before {{c1::January 1, 2026}}.
notes.back: January 1, 2026.
notes.explanation: Tax year 2025 discharges still qualify; the exclusion does not reach later discharges.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Reminders”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Qualified principal residence indebtedness can be excluded from income for discharges before January 1, 2026.

notes.front: A lender forgives $40,000 of the mortgage on Alex's main home in March 2026. Can Alex use the qualified principal residence indebtedness exclusion?
notes.back: No. It cannot be used for discharges after 2025.
notes.explanation: Publication 4681 (2025) says qualified principal residence indebtedness cannot be excluded for discharges after 2025.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Discharge of qualified principal residence indebtedness after 2025”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Discharge of qualified principal residence indebtedness after 2025. Qualified principal residence indebtedness cannot be excluded

notes.front: If a canceled debt is qualified principal residence indebtedness and you are also insolvent, which exclusion applies?
notes.back: The qualified principal residence indebtedness exclusion, unless you elect the insolvency exclusion instead.
notes.explanation: Publication 4681 makes the insolvency exclusion unavailable for such debt unless you elect it.
notes.source: Publication 4681 (2025), Canceled Debts, Foreclosures, Repossessions, and Abandonments, “Insolvency”, p. 6
notes.evidence: if the debt is qualified principal residence indebtedness (defined in this section under Qualified Principal Residence Indebtedness, later) unless you elect to apply the insolvency exclusion instead of the qualified principal residence indebtedness exclusion.

notes.front: Is a U.S. citizen living abroad taxed on foreign income?
notes.back: Generally yes: a U.S. citizen or resident alien's worldwide income is generally subject to U.S. income tax.
notes.explanation: Publication 54 says this applies regardless of where you are living.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Introduction”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you are a U.S. citizen or resident alien, your worldwide income is generally subject to U.S. income tax, regardless of where you are living.

notes.front: A U.S. citizen working in a treaty country wants to use the treaty to cut their U.S. tax. What generally stops them?
notes.back: The treaty's saving clause, which keeps U.S. taxation of its own citizens and residents unchanged.
notes.explanation: Saving clauses mean U.S. citizens and residents cannot generally use a treaty to reduce U.S. tax, though most treaties have exceptions.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Saving clauses”, p. 27
notes.evidence: U.S. treaties contain saving clauses that provide that the treaties do not affect the U.S. taxation of its own citizens and residents. As a result, U.S. citizens and residents cannot generally use the treaty to reduce their U.S. tax liability.

notes.front: Which form do you attach to your return to claim the foreign earned income exclusion?
notes.back: Form 2555.
notes.explanation: Publication 54 says the exclusion is claimed by attaching Form 2555 to Form 1040 or Form 1040-X.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Introduction”, p. 4
notes.evidence: you must file Form 2555 by attaching it to your federal income tax return, Form 1040, 1040-SR, or 1040-X.

notes.front: Which form is used for the foreign tax credit?
notes.back: Form 1116.
notes.explanation: Publication 54 refers to the allowed foreign tax credit as figured on Form 1116.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Chapter 1: penalties affecting returns”, p. 13
notes.evidence: Reduction in allowed foreign tax credit (Form 1116).

notes.front: A U.S. citizen receives a large gift from a relative who is a foreign person. Which form reports it?
notes.back: Form 3520.
notes.explanation: Form 3520 reports transactions with foreign trusts and receipt of certain large gifts or bequests from certain foreign persons.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Form 3520”, p. 13
notes.evidence: Form 3520, Annual Return To Report Transactions With Foreign Trusts and Receipt of Certain Foreign Gifts, to report: • Certain transactions with foreign trusts, • Ownership of foreign trusts

notes.front: A U.S. citizen is a director and shareholder of a company incorporated abroad. Which information return may they have to file?
notes.back: Form 5471.
notes.explanation: Certain U.S. persons who are officers, directors or shareholders in certain foreign corporations file Form 5471.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Form 5471”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Certain U.S. persons who are officers, directors, or shareholders in certain foreign corporations must file Form 5471, Information Return of U.S. Persons With Respect To Certain Foreign Corporations

notes.front: How is the housing amount for the foreign housing exclusion or deduction figured?
notes.back: Your housing expenses for the year minus the base housing amount.
notes.explanation: Only housing costs above the base amount count.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Housing Amount”, p. 19
notes.evidence: Your housing amount is the total of your housing expenses for the year minus the base housing amount.

notes.front: Who can treat a scholarship or fellowship grant as tax free?
notes.back: Only a candidate for a degree at an eligible educational institution.
notes.explanation: Degree candidacy is the first condition before looking at how the money is spent.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Scholarships and Fellowship Grants”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A scholarship or fellowship grant is tax free (excludable from gross income) only if you are a candidate for a degree at an eligible educational institution.

notes.front: For a tax-free scholarship, what are qualified education expenses?
notes.back: Tuition and fees to enroll or attend; and required course-related expenses such as fees, books, supplies and equipment.
notes.explanation: The course items must be required of all students in the course.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Qualified education expenses”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Tuition and fees required to enroll at or attend an eligible educational institution; and • Course-related expenses, such as fees, books,

notes.front: A degree student gets a $20,000 scholarship and spends $14,000 on tuition, $1,000 on required books and $5,000 on dormitory housing. How much is taxable?
notes.explanation: Qualified: $14,000 + $1,000 = $15,000. $20,000 − $15,000 = $5,000, the part used for room and board, is taxable.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Expenses that don't qualify”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Qualified education expenses don't include the cost of: • Room and board

notes.front: What do you include in income from bartering, and when?
notes.back: The fair market value of the property or services you receive, at the time you receive them.
notes.explanation: Bartering is an exchange of property or services, so the value received is the income.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Bartering”, p. 20
notes.evidence: You must include in your income, at the time received, the FMV of property or services you receive in bartering.

notes.front: A plumber agrees in advance to fix a painter's pipes in exchange for having a room painted, both valued at $600. What does each include?
notes.back: Each includes $600 in income.
notes.explanation: When both agree the value ahead of time, that value is accepted as fair market value unless shown to be otherwise.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Bartering”, p. 20
notes.evidence: If you exchange services with another person and you both have agreed ahead of time on the value of the services, that value will be accepted as FMV unless the value can be shown to be otherwise.

notes.front: Can a loss from a hobby be deducted from other income?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Publication 525 defines a hobby as an activity from which you don't expect to make a profit.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Hobby losses”, p. 34
notes.evidence: Losses from a hobby aren't deductible from other income. A hobby is an activity from which you don't expect to make a profit.

notes.front: Kim knits for fun and sold scarves for $700, spending $900 on wool. Can Kim deduct the $200 difference against wages?
notes.back: No. The $700 is reported as income, and the hobby loss can't offset other income.
notes.explanation: Hobby income goes on Schedule 1, line 8j, and losses from a hobby aren't deductible from other income.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Hobby losses”, p. 34
notes.evidence: Losses from a hobby aren't deductible from other income.

notes.front: Is alimony under a divorce instrument executed after 2018 included in the recipient's income?
notes.back: No. It is not includible by the recipient and not deductible by the payer.
notes.explanation: The same applies to a pre-2019 instrument modified after 2018 if the modification expressly adopts these rules.
notes.source: Publication 504 (2025), Divorced or Separated Individuals, “Alimony”, p. 16
notes.evidence: instrument executed after 2018 won't be deductible by the payer. Such amounts also won't be includible in the income of the recipient.

notes.front: Taylor receives alimony under a 2016 divorce decree that has never been modified. Is it taxable to Taylor in 2025?
notes.back: Yes. Alimony under an instrument executed before 2019 is included in the recipient's income.
notes.explanation: Only instruments executed after 2018, or older ones modified to adopt the new rules, leave alimony out of income.
notes.source: Publication 504 (2025), Divorced or Separated Individuals, “Alimony Payment Rules for Instruments Executed Prior to 2019”, p. 13
notes.evidence: you can deduct $1,800 as alimony and your former spouse must report $1,800 as alimony received for a divorce decree executed prior to 2019.

notes.front: An enlisted service member earns $30,000 of combat zone pay. How much is included in income?
notes.back: None of it.
notes.explanation: For enlisted members, warrant officers and commissioned warrant officers, no combat zone pay is included; commissioned officers' exclusion is limited.
notes.source: Publication 3 (2025), Armed Forces' Tax Guide, “How Much of My Combat Zone Pay Can I Exclude?”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If you are an enlisted member, warrant officer, or commissioned warrant officer, none of your combat zone pay is included in your income for tax purposes.

notes.front: Where is income from illegal activities reported?
notes.back: On Schedule 1, line 8z, or on Schedule C if it comes from a self-employment activity.
notes.explanation: Publication 525 gives money from dealing illegal drugs as an example.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Illegal activities”, p. 34
notes.evidence: Income from illegal activities, such as money from dealing illegal drugs, must be included in your income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8z, or on Schedule C (Form 1040) if from your self-employment activity.

notes.front: When is a 2025 state income tax refund included in income?
notes.back: Generally when you deducted the state tax in an earlier year; the payer sends Form 1099-G.
notes.explanation: Publication 525 ties inclusion to having deducted the tax in an earlier year; the payer should send Form 1099-G by January 31, 2026.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “State tax refund”, p. 24
notes.evidence: If you received a state or local income tax refund (or credit or offset) in 2025, you must generally include it in income if you deducted the tax in an earlier year.

notes.front: Drew took the standard deduction for 2024 and got a $600 state income tax refund in 2025. How much is income?
notes.back: None.
notes.explanation: Drew didn't itemize for 2024, so the refunded tax never reduced federal tax. The whole $600 stays out of income.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Deductions not itemized”, p. 24
notes.evidence: If you didn't itemize deductions for the year for which you received the recovery of an expense that was deductible only if you itemized, don't include any of the recovery amount in your income.

notes.front: Avery itemized for 2024, deducting state income tax, and the whole deduction reduced Avery's tax. A $900 state refund arrives in 2025. How much is income?
notes.back: The $900, generally, figured with the worksheet in the Form 1040 instructions.
notes.explanation: Under the tax benefit rule the recovery is income up to the amount the earlier deduction reduced tax, here the full $900.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “State tax refund”, p. 24
notes.evidence: you must generally include it in income if you deducted the tax in an earlier year.

notes.front: A client's courier tries to deliver a fee cheque to a cash-method freelancer on 31 December 2025, but no one is home. Which year is it income?
notes.explanation: A valid cheque made available before the end of the year is constructively received that year, even if cashed later.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Constructively received income”, p. 2
notes.evidence: A valid check that you received or that was made available to you before the end of the tax year is considered income constructively received in that year

notes.front: A payer mails a cheque on 31 December 2025 so that it cannot reach the cash-method recipient until January, and the funds are unavailable before then. Which year is it income?
notes.back: 2026, the next tax year.
notes.explanation: The money was not available in 2025, so it was not constructively received that year.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Constructively received income”, p. 2
notes.evidence: If the check was mailed so that it couldn't possibly reach you until after the end of the tax year, and you otherwise couldn't get the funds before the end of the year, you include the amount in your income for the next tax year.

notes.front: When are constructive distributions from a corporation taxable?
notes.back: When they have the same result as one of the taxable stock distributions Publication 550 lists.
notes.explanation: Examples include a change in conversion ratio or redemption price that increases your proportionate interest.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Constructive distributions”, p. 31
notes.evidence: These constructive distributions are taxable if they have the same result as a distribution described in (2), (3), (4), or (5) of the above discussion.

notes.front: Is a passive activity loss generally allowed for the year?
notes.back: Generally no, though a special $25,000 allowance may allow some or all of it.
notes.explanation: The passive activity loss is the excess of passive deductions over passive gross income.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Passive Activity Loss”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Generally, the passive activity loss for the tax year isn't allowed. However, there is a special allowance under which some or all of your passive activity loss may be allowed.

notes.front: Casey, not a real estate professional, manages a rental house personally for 600 hours a year. Is the rental passive?
notes.back: Yes. Rental activities are passive even with material participation, unless you are a real estate professional.
notes.explanation: The 500-hour test matters for trade or business activities, not rentals.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Passive Activities”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Rental activities, even if you do materially participate in them, unless you're a real estate professional.

notes.front: Which material participation test can a sole worker meet with few hours?
notes.back: Your participation was substantially all the participation of all individuals in the activity for the year.
notes.explanation: It counts people who own no interest in the activity too.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Material participation tests”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Your participation was substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals for the tax year, including the participation of individuals who didn't own any interest in the activity.

notes.front: Which material participation test uses 100 hours?
notes.back: More than 100 hours in the year, and at least as much as any other individual.
notes.explanation: Both parts must be met.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Material participation tests”, p. 7
notes.evidence: You participated in the activity for more than 100 hours during the tax year, and you participated at least as much as any other individual

notes.front: Which material participation test looks at significant participation activities?
notes.back: Participating in all significant participation activities combined for more than 500 hours.
notes.explanation: The activity itself must be a significant participation activity.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Material participation tests”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The activity is a significant participation activity, and you participated in all significant participation activities combined for more than 500 hours.

notes.front: Riley worked 120 hours in a food truck business; the only other worker put in 110 hours. Does Riley materially participate?
notes.back: Yes, under the more-than-100-hours test.
notes.explanation: 120 hours is more than 100, and 120 is at least as much as the other worker's 110.
notes.source: Publication 925 (2025), Passive Activity and At-Risk Rules, “Material participation tests”, p. 7
notes.evidence: You participated in the activity for more than 100 hours during the tax year, and you participated at least as much as any other individual

notes.front: A trust must distribute all its current income each year but paid Elliot nothing in 2025. Must Elliot report a share of its income?
notes.back: Yes. Elliot reports the share of distributable net income whether or not it was actually received.
notes.explanation: For an estate or trust that must distribute all current income, the beneficiary's share is reported regardless of payment; it comes on Schedule K-1 (Form 1041).
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Current income required to be distributed”, p. 32
notes.evidence: If you're the beneficiary of an estate or trust that must distribute all of its current income, you must report your share of the distributable net income, whether or not you actually received it.

notes.front: What limits the partnership losses a partner can deduct?
notes.back: The adjusted basis of the partnership interest at the end of the partnership year in which the losses took place.
notes.explanation: Losses above that basis can't be deducted that year.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Partnership Income”, p. 17
notes.evidence: share of the partnership losses is limited to the adjusted basis of your partnership interest at the end of the partnership year in which the losses took place.

notes.front: How are royalties from copyrights, patents and oil, gas and mineral properties taxed, and where are they usually reported?
notes.back: As ordinary income, in most cases on Schedule E.
notes.explanation: Self-employed writers, inventors and artists, or holders of operating oil, gas or mineral interests, use Schedule C.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Royalties”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Royalties from copyrights; patents; and oil, gas, and mineral properties are taxable as ordinary income. In most cases, you report royalties on Schedule E (Form 1040).

notes.front: For 2025, when must a payment app or online marketplace send you Form 1099-K?
notes.back: Only if your business transactions total more than $20,000 and number more than 200.
notes.explanation: Both the dollar and the transaction-count thresholds must be exceeded.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Updated reporting requirements for Form 1099-K”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Payment card companies, payment apps, and online marketplaces will be required to send you a Form 1099-K only if the amount of your business transactions during the year is more than $20,000 and the total number of your transactions is more than 200.

notes.front: A seller had $9,000 of business sales through an app in 2025 and received no Form 1099-K. Must the income be reported?
notes.back: Yes. Income is reported whether or not a Form 1099-K was received.
notes.explanation: The $9,000 is under the $20,000 threshold, so no form is required, but the income is still taxable.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Self-employment income”, p. 28
notes.evidence: whether you received a Form 1099-K, Payment Card and Third Party Network Transactions, or not.

notes.front: A shop pays an independent bookkeeper $550 in 2025. Must the shop send a Form 1099-NEC, and is the $550 taxable?
notes.back: No form is required below $600, but the $550 is still income to the bookkeeper.
notes.explanation: The Form 1099-NEC threshold is $600 or more; the duty to report income does not depend on the form.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Nonemployee compensation”, p. 77
notes.evidence: total $600 or more for the year, the payer should send you a Form 1099-NEC. You may need to report your fees as self-employment income.

notes.front: How can you tell a Form 1099 is a corrected form?
notes.back: It has an "X" in the "CORRECTED" box at the top.
notes.explanation: A corrected Form W-2 is a different form, Form W-2c.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Form W-2G or 1099 incorrect”, p. 46
notes.evidence: The corrected Form W-2G or Form 1099 you receive will have an "X" in the "CORRECTED" box at the top of the form.

notes.front: Must a Roth IRA owner take required minimum distributions during life?
notes.back: No. The minimum distribution rules don't apply to Roth IRAs while the owner is alive.
notes.explanation: After the owner's death, some minimum distribution rules do apply to beneficiaries.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Are Distributions Taxable? (Roth IRAs)”, p. 37
notes.evidence: You aren't required to take distributions from your Roth IRA at any age. The minimum distribution rules that apply to traditional IRAs don't apply to Roth IRAs while the owner is alive.

notes.front: For 2025, at what modified adjusted gross income can a single filer no longer contribute to a Roth IRA?
notes.back: $165,000 or more; the reduction starts at $150,000.
notes.explanation: Contributions are reduced between $150,000 and $165,000 for single filers.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What's New for 2025”, p. 2
notes.evidence: 2025 and your modified AGI is at least $150,000. You can't make a Roth IRA contribution if your modified AGI is $165,000 or more.

notes.front: Two savers each put $7,000 into an IRA in 2025, one traditional and one Roth. Whose contribution may be deductible, and whose qualified withdrawals are tax free?
notes.back: The traditional saver may deduct; the Roth saver gets tax-free qualified distributions.
notes.explanation: Roth contributions are never deductible, but qualified Roth distributions are tax free; traditional IRAs defer tax instead.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “What Is a Roth IRA?”, p. 39
notes.evidence: Unlike a traditional IRA, you can't deduct contributions to a Roth IRA. But, if you satisfy the requirements, qualified distributions (discussed in chapter 2 of Pub. 590-B) are tax free

notes.front: Must you file Form 8606 for nondeductible IRA contributions if you have no filing requirement?
notes.back: Yes. Form 8606 reports nondeductible contributions even if you don't have to file a tax return.
notes.explanation: The form records your basis, the after-tax money already in the IRA.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Nondeductible Contributions”, p. 16
notes.evidence: You must file Form 8606 to report nondeductible contributions even if you don't have to file a tax return for the year.

notes.front: Jamie contributes $7,000 to a traditional IRA for 2025 but can deduct only $3,000. What is nondeductible, and what form records it?
notes.back: $4,000 nondeductible, reported on Form 8606.
notes.explanation: $7,000 permitted − $3,000 deduction = $4,000. That amount becomes basis, recovered tax free when distributed.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Nondeductible Contributions”, p. 16
notes.evidence: The difference between your total permitted contributions and your IRA deduction, if any, is your nondeductible contribution.

notes.front: To recover your IRA basis when you take a distribution, what must you complete?
notes.back: Form 8606 for the year of the distribution.
notes.explanation: Nondeductible contributions become basis, and Form 8606 works out the tax-free part of each distribution.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Nondeductible contributions”, p. 26
notes.evidence: To recover your basis when you take distributions from your IRA, you must complete Form 8606 for the year of the distribution.

notes.front: After a tax-free rollover from a traditional IRA, when can you roll over a later distribution from that same IRA?
notes.back: Not within 1 year of the date you received the first distribution.
notes.explanation: The same 1-year wait applies to the IRA that received the rollover.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Waiting period between rollovers”, p. 25
notes.evidence: if you make a tax-free rollover of any part of a distribution from a traditional IRA, you can't, within a 1-year period, make a tax-free rollover of any later distribution from that same IRA.

notes.front: For an eligible distribution from an employer plan, what withholding applies if it is paid to you rather than directly rolled over?
notes.back: The payer must withhold 20% of the taxable part; a direct rollover has no withholding.
notes.explanation: Publication 590-A's table contrasts a payment to you with a direct rollover.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Table 1-5. Comparison of Payment to You Versus Direct Rollover”, p. 27
notes.evidence: The payer must withhold 20% of the taxable part. There is no withholding.

notes.front: Noa withdrew $5,000 from an IRA on 1 March 2025 and deposited it in another IRA on 15 May 2025. Is it a tax-free rollover?
notes.back: No. It was contributed more than 60 days after the distribution.
notes.explanation: 1 March to 15 May is 75 days, beyond the 60-day limit for a rollover.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Rollovers”, p. 22
notes.evidence: a rollover is a tax-free distribution to you of cash or other assets from one retirement plan that you contribute to another retirement plan within 60 days

notes.front: What does code 1 in box 7 of Form 1099-R mean?
notes.back: Early distribution, no known exception (in most cases, under age 59½).
notes.explanation: Code 1 points you to the rules on early distributions and the additional tax.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Number codes”, p. 21
notes.evidence: 1—Early distribution, no known exception (in most case

notes.front: What does code G on Form 1099-R mean?
notes.back: A direct rollover to a qualified plan, section 403(b) plan, governmental section 457(b) plan or IRA.
notes.explanation: A direct rollover isn't taxable when made.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Letter codes”, p. 21
notes.evidence: G—Direct rollover of a distribution to a qualified plan, a section 403(b) plan, a governmental section 457(b) plan, or an IRA.

notes.front: A Form 1099-R shows code 5. Which rules should the preparer look at?
notes.back: The prohibited transaction rules.
notes.explanation: Code 5 points to prohibited transactions; code 8 points to excess contributions.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Number codes”, p. 21
notes.evidence: If code 5 appears, see Prohibited Transactions, later. If code 8 appears, see Excess Contributions

notes.front: To make a qualified charitable distribution you must be at least age {{c1::70½}} when it is made.
notes.explanation: This is younger than the age at which required minimum distributions begin.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs)”, p. 13
notes.evidence: You must be at least age 701/2 when the distribution is made.

notes.front: What is the 2025 maximum annual exclusion for qualified charitable distributions, and what happens above it?
notes.back: $108,000; any excess is included in income like any other distribution.
notes.explanation: The cap applies to the exclusion, not to the giving itself.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs)”, p. 14
notes.evidence: The maximum annual exclusion for QCDs is $108,000. Any QCD in excess of the $108,000 exclusion limit is included in income as any other distribution.

notes.front: Lou, 75, has a $12,000 RMD for 2025 and has the IRA trustee pay $12,000 directly to a qualifying charity, with the usual acknowledgment. How much of it is taxable?
notes.back: None. It is a qualified charitable distribution and it also meets the RMD.
notes.explanation: Lou is over 70½, the trustee paid the charity directly, and $12,000 is under the $108,000 limit.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs)”, p. 13
notes.evidence: A QCD is generally a nontaxable distribution made directly by the trustee of your IRA (other than an ongoing SEP or SIMPLE IRA) to an organization eligible to receive tax-deductible contributions.

notes.front: By when must a 2025 excess IRA contribution be withdrawn to avoid the 6% tax?
notes.back: By the due date of the 2025 return, including extensions: April 15, 2026, or later if the return is extended.
notes.explanation: The deadline is the 2025 return due date, extensions included.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Excess contributions”, p. 32
notes.evidence: if any 2025 excess contribution is withdrawn by April 15, 2026 (including extensions).

notes.front: Val, 30, earned $4,500 of wages in 2025 and put $7,000 into a traditional IRA. What is the excess contribution?
notes.explanation: The limit is the smaller of $7,000 or taxable compensation of $4,500. $7,000 − $4,500 = $2,500 excess.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Excess Contributions”, p. 35
notes.evidence: Generally, an excess contribution is the amount contributed to your traditional IRAs for the year that is more than the smaller of:

notes.front: What additional tax generally applies to IRA withdrawals before age 59½?
notes.back: A 10% additional tax.
notes.explanation: Publication 590-B explains it under the age 59½ rule for early distributions.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Can You Move Retirement Plan Assets? / Early Distributions”, p. 6
notes.evidence: a 10% additional tax generally applies if you withdraw or use IRA assets before you reach age 591/2.

notes.front: Mo, 40, takes $8,000 from a fully deductible traditional IRA to buy a car. No exception applies. What is the additional tax?
notes.back: $800, on top of regular income tax on the $8,000.
notes.explanation: 10% × $8,000 = $800. Buying a car is not an exception.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Early distributions”, p. 6
notes.evidence: a 10% additional tax generally applies if you withdraw or use IRA assets before you reach age 591/2.

notes.front: Which medical exception can avoid the 10% additional tax on an early IRA distribution?
notes.back: Unreimbursed medical expenses that are more than 7.5% of your adjusted gross income.
notes.explanation: It is one of several exceptions to the age 59½ rule.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: You have unreimbursed medical expenses that are more than 7.5% of your AGI.

notes.front: Which early distribution exception relates to a period of unemployment?
notes.back: A distribution for the cost of your medical insurance due to a period of unemployment.
notes.explanation: The distribution must be for medical insurance.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: The distribution is for the cost of your medical insurance due to a period of unemployment.

notes.front: Pia, 50, is totally and permanently disabled and withdraws $15,000 from her IRA. Does the 10% additional tax apply?
notes.back: No. Total and permanent disability is an exception.
notes.explanation: The distribution is still subject to regular income tax.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: You are totally and permanently disabled.

notes.front: Which early distribution exception involves a medical certification?
notes.back: Being certified as having a terminal illness.
notes.explanation: It sits beside the disability exception in the list.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: You have been certified as having a terminal illness.

notes.front: Ty, 35, inherits an IRA from an aunt and withdraws $20,000. Does the 10% additional tax apply?
notes.back: No. A beneficiary of a deceased IRA owner is excepted.
notes.explanation: Ty's age does not matter for this exception.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: You are the beneficiary of a deceased IRA owner.

notes.front: Which early distribution exception involves a pattern of payments?
notes.back: Receiving distributions as a series of substantially equal payments.
notes.explanation: The payments must follow the substantially equal pattern.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: You are receiving distributions in the form of a series of substantially equal

notes.front: A 30-year-old first-time buyer uses an IRA distribution to buy a first home. Which exception may apply?
notes.back: The exception for distributions to buy, build or rebuild a first home.
notes.explanation: Publication 590-B lists first-home distributions among the exceptions; limits apply.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: distributions to buy, build, or rebuild a first home.

notes.front: Is an early IRA distribution caused by an IRS levy on the IRA subject to the 10% additional tax?
notes.back: No. A distribution due to an IRS levy of the IRA is an exception.
notes.explanation: The levy exception is listed with the other exceptions.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: The distribution is due to an IRS levy of the IRA.

notes.front: Which early distribution exception relates to a new child?
notes.back: A qualified birth or adoption distribution.
notes.explanation: It is one of the listed exceptions to the age 59½ rule.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: The distribution is a qualified birth or adoption distribution.

notes.front: Which two exceptions to the 10% additional tax relate to reserve military service and to disasters?
notes.back: A qualified reservist distribution; a qualified disaster recovery distribution.
notes.explanation: Both appear in Publication 590-B's list of exceptions to the age 59½ rule.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Exceptions”, p. 24
notes.evidence: The distribution is a qualified reservist distribution. • The distribution is a qualified birth or adoption distribution. • The distribution is a qualified disaster recovery distribution.

notes.front: Val takes a personal loan from her own traditional IRA. Is that a prohibited transaction?
notes.back: Yes. Borrowing money from it is a prohibited transaction.
notes.explanation: Borrowing money from the IRA is on Publication 590-B's list of examples.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Prohibited Transactions”, p. 22
notes.evidence: The following are some examples of prohibited transactions with a traditional IRA. • Borrowing money from it.

notes.front: An IRA owner sells a rental building he owns personally to his own IRA. Is that a prohibited transaction?
notes.back: Yes. Selling property to the IRA is a prohibited transaction.
notes.explanation: Selling property to it is one of the listed examples.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Prohibited Transactions”, p. 22
notes.evidence: Borrowing money from it. • Selling property to it. • Using it as security for a loan.

notes.front: If you engage in a prohibited transaction with your IRA, when does the account stop being an IRA?
notes.back: As of the first day of the year in which the transaction happened.
notes.explanation: With several IRAs, only the one involved loses its status.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Effect on an IRA account”, p. 22
notes.evidence: Generally, if you or your beneficiary engages in a prohibited transaction in connection with your IRA account at any time during the year, the account stops being an IRA as of the first day of that year.

notes.front: After a prohibited transaction ends IRA status, what is treated as distributed to you?
notes.back: All the account's assets, at their fair market values on the first day of the year.
notes.explanation: The whole account is treated as paid out, not just the amount involved.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Effect on you or your beneficiary”, p. 22
notes.evidence: the account is treated as distributing all its assets to you at their fair market values on the first day

notes.front: Nico has two traditional IRAs worth $40,000 and $60,000 on 1 January 2025. In June he borrows from the $40,000 one. What is treated as distributed?
notes.back: $40,000, the first IRA's value on 1 January 2025; the $60,000 IRA keeps its status.
notes.explanation: Each IRA is a separate account, and the one involved is treated as distributing all its assets at 1 January values.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Effect on an IRA account”, p. 22
notes.evidence: if you own more than one IRA, each IRA is treated as a separate account, and loss of IRA status only affects the IRA that participated in the prohibited transaction.

notes.front: Is a traditional-to-Roth conversion taxable?
notes.back: Part or all of it may be included in gross income, but the 10% early distribution tax doesn't apply if properly rolled over.
notes.explanation: The conversion is a taxable move, not a penalty event.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Converting From Any Traditional IRA Into a Roth IRA”, p. 29
notes.evidence: If properly (and timely) rolled over, the 10% additional tax on early distributions won't apply. However, a part or all of the distribution from your traditional IRA may be included in gross income

notes.front: Sky, 45, converts $30,000 from a traditional IRA with no basis to a Roth IRA in 2025. How much is taxable, and is there a 10% additional tax?
notes.back: $30,000 is taxable income; no 10% additional tax.
notes.explanation: With no basis, the whole $30,000 is included in gross income. A proper conversion avoids the 10% additional tax.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Converting From Any Traditional IRA Into a Roth IRA”, p. 29
notes.evidence: If properly (and timely) rolled over, the 10% additional tax on early distributions won't apply.

notes.front: By when must a recharacterization transfer be made?
notes.back: By the due date, including extensions, of the return for the year the contribution was made.
notes.explanation: If timely, you can elect to treat the contribution as made to the second IRA.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Recharacterizations”, p. 29
notes.evidence: If the transfer is made by the due date (including extensions) for your tax return for the tax year for which the contribution was made, you can elect to treat the contribution as having been originally made to the second IRA

notes.front: Ellis, single, contributed $7,000 to a Roth IRA for 2025, then found their modified AGI was $170,000, too high for Roth contributions. What can Ellis do by the 2025 return due date?
notes.back: Recharacterize the contribution as a traditional IRA contribution by trustee-to-trustee transfer.
notes.explanation: $170,000 exceeds the $165,000 single ceiling. A timely transfer lets the contribution be treated as made to a traditional IRA.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Recharacterizations”, p. 29
notes.evidence: To recharacterize a contribution, you must generally have the contribution transferred from the first IRA (the one to which it was made) to the second IRA in a trustee-to-trustee transfer.

notes.front: For someone who reaches 72 after 2022, by when must required minimum distributions begin?
notes.back: By April 1 of the year after the year they reach age 73.
notes.explanation: Publication 590-B calls this the required beginning date for tax years 2023 and later.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Age 73 for tax years 2023 and later”, p. 6
notes.evidence: If you reach age 72 after December 31, 2022, you must begin receiving required minimum distributions by April 1 of the year following the year you reach the age 73.

notes.front: Gale turns 73 in 2025. What is the latest date for the first required minimum distribution?
notes.back: April 1, 2026.
notes.explanation: The required beginning date is April 1 of the year after the year you reach 73: 2025 + 1 = 2026.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Age 73 for tax years 2023 and later”, p. 6
notes.evidence: you must begin receiving required minimum distributions by April 1 of the year following the year you reach the age 73.

notes.front: What excise tax applies to an RMD not taken, and when can it drop?
notes.back: 25% of the amount not distributed; 10% if corrected within the correction window.
notes.explanation: The reduced rate needs the shortfall distributed and a return reflecting the tax in the window.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Excess Accumulations (Insufficient Distributions)”, p. 30
notes.evidence: you may have to pay a 25% excise tax for that year on the amount not distributed as required. Reduced additional tax rate for excess accumulations. You may be subject to a reduced additional tax rate of 10% of the amount not distributed

notes.front: Ray's 2025 RMD was $10,000 but he took only $4,000 and did not correct it. What excise tax may apply?
notes.explanation: $10,000 − $4,000 = $6,000 not distributed. 25% × $6,000 = $1,500; correcting within the window could cut it to 10%, or $600.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Excess Accumulations (Insufficient Distributions)”, p. 30
notes.evidence: you may have to pay a 25% excise tax for that year on the amount not distributed as required.

notes.front: How is a loan from your retirement plan generally treated?
notes.back: As a nonperiodic distribution, unless it meets the exception.
notes.explanation: The rule covers qualified and nonqualified plans, including commercial annuities.
notes.source: Publication 575 (2025), Pension and Annuity Income, “Loans Treated as Distributions”, p. 18
notes.evidence: If you borrow money from your retirement plan, you must treat the loan as a nonperiodic distribution from the plan unless it qualifies for the exception to this loan-as-distribution rule explained later.

notes.front: Which plan loans can qualify for the exception to the loan-as-distribution rule?
