notes.back: A loan used to acquire your main home, or one that must be repaid within 5 years.
notes.explanation: Even then, only the amount within the dollar limits escapes distribution treatment.
notes.source: Publication 575 (2025), Pension and Annuity Income, “Exception”, p. 18
notes.evidence: This exception to the loan-as-distribution rule applies only to a loan that either: • Is used to acquire your main home, or • Must be repaid within 5 years.

notes.front: Dev, with a $200,000 vested balance and no other loans, borrows $60,000 from a 401(k), repayable over 5 years. How much is treated as a distribution?
notes.source: Publication 575 (2025), Pension and Annuity Income, “Exception”, p. 18
notes.evidence: exceeds the lesser of: • $50,000; or • Half the present value (but not less than $10,000) of your nonforfeitable accrued benefit under the plan

notes.front: What do you compare with your base amount to see if benefits may be taxable?
notes.back: One-half of your benefits plus all your other income, including tax-exempt interest.
notes.explanation: If the total is more than the base amount, part of the benefits may be taxable.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Are Any of Your Benefits Taxable?”, p. 3
notes.evidence: To figure the total of one-half of your benefits plus your other income, use Worksheet A, discussed later. If the total is more than your base amount, part of your benefits may be taxable.

notes.front: The social security base amount is {{c1::$25,000}} for single, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse filers.
notes.explanation: It is the threshold the half-benefits-plus-other-income total is compared with.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Base amount”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Your base amount is: • $25,000 if you are single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse;

notes.front: For married filing jointly, the social security base amount is {{c1::$32,000}}.
notes.explanation: A joint return combines both spouses' incomes and benefits against this amount.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Base amount”, p. 3
notes.evidence: $32,000 if you are married filing jointly;

notes.front: What is the base amount for a married filing separately taxpayer who lived apart from the spouse all of 2025?
notes.explanation: Living apart all year gives the same base as a single filer.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Base amount”, p. 3
notes.evidence: $25,000 if you are married filing separately and lived apart from your spouse for all of 2025;

notes.front: What is the base amount for a married filing separately taxpayer who lived with the spouse at any time in 2025?
notes.explanation: Such a taxpayer also falls into the up-to-85% rule.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Base amount”, p. 3
notes.evidence: $0 if you are married filing separately and lived with your spouse at any time during 2025.

notes.front: When can up to 85% of benefits be taxable?
notes.back: When half your benefits plus other income exceeds $34,000 ($44,000 married filing jointly), or you file separately and lived with your spouse.
notes.explanation: These are the two situations Publication 915 lists.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Maximum taxable part”, p. 6
notes.evidence: up to 85% of your benefits can be taxable if either of the following situations applies to you. • The total of one-half of your benefits and all your other income is more than $34,000 ($44,000 if you are married filing jointly).

notes.front: Single filer Bo received $20,000 of benefits and $20,000 of pension income in 2025. Could any benefits be taxable?
notes.back: Yes. The $30,000 total is over the $25,000 base amount.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Base amount”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Your base amount is: • $25,000 if you are single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse;

notes.front: A married couple filing jointly got $24,000 of benefits and have $18,000 of other income. Are any benefits taxable?
notes.back: No. Their $30,000 total is under the $32,000 base amount.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Base amount”, p. 3
notes.evidence: $32,000 if you are married filing jointly;

notes.front: Single filer Cam's half-benefits-plus-other-income total is $40,000. What is the maximum share of benefits that can be taxable?
notes.back: Up to 85%.
notes.explanation: $40,000 is more than $34,000, the single threshold for the 85% ceiling.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Maximum taxable part”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The total of one-half of your benefits and all your other income is more than $34,000 ($44,000 if you are married filing jointly).

notes.front: Single filer Jo's half-benefits-plus-other-income total is $29,000. What is the maximum share of benefits that can be taxable?
notes.back: Up to 50%.
notes.explanation: $29,000 is above the $25,000 base but not above $34,000, so the general 50% ceiling applies.
notes.source: Publication 915 (2025), Social Security and Equivalent Railroad Retirement Benefits, “Maximum taxable part”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Generally, up to 50% of your benefits will be taxable.

notes.front: Under the 10-year rule, by when must an inherited IRA be emptied?
notes.back: By December 31 of the year containing the 10th anniversary of the owner's death.
notes.explanation: It applies to beneficiaries who are not taking life expectancy payments.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “10-year rule”, p. 10
notes.evidence: The 10-year rule requires the IRA beneficiaries who are not taking life expectancy payments to withdraw the entire balance of the IRA by December 31 of the year containing the 10th anniversary of the owner's death.

notes.front: Rae's uncle died in 2024; Rae, 30, is a designated beneficiary but not an eligible designated beneficiary. By when must the inherited IRA be fully distributed?
notes.back: By December 31, 2034.
notes.explanation: The 10th anniversary of a 2024 death falls in 2034, so the balance must be out by 31 December 2034.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “10-year rule”, p. 10
notes.evidence: (2) the beneficiary is a designated beneficiary who is not an eligible

notes.front: Who is an eligible designated beneficiary of an IRA?
notes.back: The surviving spouse, the owner's minor child, a disabled or chronically ill person, or someone not more than 10 years younger than the owner.
notes.explanation: These beneficiaries can use life expectancy payments instead of the 10-year rule in many cases.
notes.source: Publication 590-B (2025), Distributions from Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Eligible designated beneficiary”, p. 9
notes.evidence: the owner's surviving spouse, the owner's minor child, a disabled individual, a chronically ill individual, or any other individual who is not more than 10 years younger than the IRA owner.

notes.front: How must a nonspouse designated beneficiary roll over an employer plan distribution?
notes.back: By a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into an inherited IRA.
notes.explanation: A nonspouse beneficiary cannot roll it into their own IRA.
notes.source: Publication 590-A (2025), Contributions to Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), “Rollover by nonspouse beneficiary”, p. 26
notes.evidence: You must make the rollover by a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into an inherited IRA.

notes.front: When can an employer's contributions to a foreign retirement plan be part of your cost in the plan?
notes.back: Only if they would have been excludable from your gross income had they been paid to you directly as compensation.
notes.explanation: Cost in the plan is recovered tax free, so only such contributions count.
notes.source: Publication 575 (2025), Pension and Annuity Income, “Foreign employment contributions”, p. 11
notes.evidence: If you worked abroad, your cost may include contributions by your employer to the retirement plan, but only if those contributions would be excludable from your gross income had they been paid directly to you as compensation.

notes.front: Do you include anything in income when you exercise a statutory stock option?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: For the alternative minimum tax, though, an ISO's spread at exercise can be an adjustment.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Exercise of option”, p. 12
notes.evidence: If you exercise a statutory stock option, don't include any amount in income when you exercise the option.

notes.front: What is the holding period requirement for stock from a statutory option?
notes.back: Don't sell until the later of 1 year after the stock was transferred to you or 2 years after the option was granted.
notes.explanation: A sale for conflict-of-interest reasons counts as meeting it.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Holding period requirement”, p. 12
notes.evidence: You satisfy the holding period requirement if you don't sell the stock until the end of the later of the 1-year period after the stock was transferred to you or the 2-year period after the option was granted.

notes.front: If ISO stock is sold at a gain before meeting the holding period, how much of the gain is ordinary income?
notes.back: Up to the excess of the stock's fair market value at exercise over the option price; any rest is capital gain.
notes.explanation: Your employer should report that ordinary income as wages in box 1 of Form W-2.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Holding period requirement not satisfied”, p. 12
notes.evidence: the gain is ordinary income up to the amount by which the stock's FMV when you exercised the option exceeded the option price. Any excess gain is capital gain.

notes.front: Ren exercised ISOs at $10 a share when the stock was worth $30, then sold 6 months later at $40. Per share, how much is ordinary income and how much capital gain?
notes.back: $20 ordinary income and $10 capital gain per share.
notes.explanation: The holding period was not met. $30 − $10 = $20 is ordinary; the total gain $40 − $10 = $30, so $30 − $20 = $10 is capital gain.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Holding period requirement not satisfied”, p. 12
notes.evidence: the gain is ordinary income up to the amount by which the stock's FMV when you exercised the option exceeded the option price. Any excess gain is capital gain.

notes.front: A private company grants Wren nonstatutory options that are not traded and have no readily determinable value. When does Wren have income?
notes.back: Not at grant; only when the option is exercised or transferred.
notes.explanation: Without a readily determinable value at grant, there is no income until exercise or transfer.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Option without readily determinable value”, p. 11
notes.evidence: If the FMV of the option isn't readily determinable at the time it's granted to you (even if it's determined later), you don't have income until you exercise or transfer the option.

notes.front: An employee exercises two options the same day: an ISO and a nonstatutory option with no readily determinable value. Which exercise creates income?
notes.back: The nonstatutory option exercise; exercising the ISO creates none.
notes.explanation: A statutory option is not taxed at exercise, while a nonstatutory option without a readily determinable value is taxed at exercise or transfer.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Option without readily determinable value”, p. 11
notes.evidence: you don't have income until you exercise or transfer the option.

notes.front: For an ESPP option priced at 85% to 100% of the share value at grant, what compensation arises on a sale after the holding period?
notes.back: The lesser of: fair market value at grant minus option price, or fair market value at disposition minus option price.
notes.explanation: It applies when the option was granted at a discount and the holding period was met, or the owner died holding the share.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Option granted at a discount”, p. 13
notes.evidence: If, at the time the option was granted, the option price per share was less than 100% (but not less than 85%) of the FMV of the share, and you dispose of the share after meeting the holding period requirement

notes.front: An ESPP option was granted at $17 when the share was worth $20. After meeting the holding period, the employee sells at $26. How much is compensation per share?
notes.explanation: Grant-date spread: $20 − $17 = $3. Sale-date spread: $26 − $17 = $9. The lesser, $3, is compensation; the rest of the gain is capital gain.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Option granted at a discount”, p. 13
notes.evidence: you must include in your income as compensation the lesser of: • The excess of the FMV of the share at the time the option was granted over the option price, or
